paragraphs.text: Parcelbird Now: should we launch quick-commerce grocery delivery in 2027?
Board discussion document, January 2027 meeting
Parcelbird
Board (two founders, two investors)
Synthetic benchmark data: the company, competitors and every figure are fictional

slides.title: Key questions

paragraphs.text: Key questions
Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service in three Midwest cities, in 2027, and still reach profit within its $12.0M of cash?
Is quick commerce a market that operators can serve at a profit?
Can a Parcelbird dark store earn a contribution profit per order by month 18?
Does Parcelbird run sites and win customers better than benchmark operators?
Does the launch fit within today's $12.0M and 12 months of runway?
What should Parcelbird do in 2027 instead, and when would it look again?
Decision maker
Success criteria
Timing
Out of scope
The board (two founders, two investors), deciding to approve or reject the launch
A path to profitability within today's $12.0M of cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; A contribution profit per order by month 18, as the founders' plan promises
Board meeting, January 2027
Cities beyond Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City; Raising a new funding round; The detailed software product roadmap

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: dark stores lose money and the plan breaks the runway rule; grow the software instead
Quick commerce grows fast, but its operators lose money on every order
–	US quick-commerce sales grew 2.8 times from 2022 to 2025
–	Zipcart's best city needed a $3.99 fee and lost 14% of orders
A median dark store loses $6.2 an order; the plan needs inputs no site has reached
–	The best basket and density combined still lose $1.8 an order
–	Zipcart's fee and promotion cuts still leave a $1.05 loss an order
Parcelbird's own pop-up ran below the benchmark, and few customers stayed
–	The pop-up lost about $12.6 on every order it delivered
–	Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three
The plan needs $9.5M, but only $7.2M can be spent within the runway rule
–	At the benchmark median, nine stores would lose $18.2M a year
Grow the software business instead; revisit only if a real site passes four gates
–	The nine late-stage deals are worth $864K a year, more than the hires
